My recommendation is one sentence and then I will defend it. We should move the whole workshop budget into coverage and stop spending on anything else in that segment. That is advice, and you can disagree with it. The next part is not advice. We have to sign the distributor contracts before the fifteenth, because that is in the contract and nobody in this room can move it. And there is one thing we must not do, and I want to be very clear about it, because it is the concern I hear most often. We must not cut the price to buy coverage. If we buy the first sale with a discount, we teach the workshop what our product is worth, and we do not get that back. The issue is not whether the approach works. It is whether we have the patience for the eighteen months it takes.

There is a difference between should and must that nobody teaches and everybody feels. Should is an invitation. It says here is what I think, and it leaves the door open, and that is exactly right when you want the room to argue with you, because a recommendation that survives an argument is worth four that did not have one. Must is a door closing. It says this is not up for discussion, and the moment you use it you have spent something. So spend it rarely. The people I have watched lose a room are almost always the ones who arrived with everything at must. Everything was critical, everything was non negotiable, and after twenty minutes the room stopped hearing the difference, which means the one thing that really was non negotiable arrived sounding like all the others.

The question that comes up in every lubricants strategy meeting is what to do about the independent workshop, and the honest answer is that there is no cheap way in. You have to earn the counter. The mechanic is the person who decides, and he decides in front of a customer who is already impatient, so he recommends what he trusts and what he has in his hand. Companies have tried to buy that position with discounts for thirty years, and the pattern is always the same. The discount moves volume for two quarters and then the volume goes wherever the next discount is. What works is slower and it is not complicated. Show up, train the mechanic, and be the brand that answers the phone when a customer complains. That takes about eighteen months per region, and there is no version of it that takes six.
